name: Guru Tegh Bahadur
summary: Born in 1621, Guru Tegh Bahadur founded Anandpur Sahib, travelled widely, and composed 116 hymns found in the Guru Granth Sahib. He was executed in Delhi in 1675 and is honoured as a protector of freedom of conscience.
about: Tegh Bahadur was born as Tyag Mal on 1 April 1621 in Amritsar, the youngest son of Guru Hargobind. According to Sikh tradition he received his new name after showing great courage in the Battle of Kartarpur in 1635. After Guru Har Krishan died in 1664, he was recognised as the ninth Guru in Bakala and founded Anandpur Sahib in 1665 (first called Chakk Nanaki). He travelled through north and east India, even to Assam, and Sikh accounts say he dug wells and set up community kitchens along the way. His hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib speak of calm, letting go of fear and fame. Sikh tradition says a group of Kashmiri Pandits came to him for help against pressure to change faith; the historian Satish Chandra notes no contemporary source confirms that persecution. Arrested in 1675, he was beheaded in Delhi's Chandni Chowk on 11 November 1675 after refusing to give up his beliefs.
kidSummary: Guru Tegh Bahadur was the ninth Sikh Guru. His name means brave one with the sword. He travelled to many places, started a city called Anandpur Sahib, and wrote beautiful hymns. He is remembered for standing up so that people could follow their own faith.

story.title: A boy called Tyag Mal
story.text: Tegh Bahadur was born in Amritsar as the youngest son of Guru Hargobind. As a boy he practised archery and riding and also studied old books.

story.title: A new name
story.text: After he fought bravely in a battle in 1635, he was given the name Tegh Bahadur, which means brave wielder of the sword.

story.title: Finding the true Guru
story.text: When Guru Har Krishan passed away, many men in Bakala said they were the next Guru. A merchant named Makhan Shah checked each one and found Tegh Bahadur was the real Guru.

story.title: Travels and kindness
story.text: The Guru travelled across north and east India. Sikh tradition says he helped dig wells and start free kitchens for people who needed food.

story.title: A stand for freedom
story.text: In 1675 he was brought to Delhi and chose not to give up his faith. Sikhs remember him for defending the right of people to follow their own beliefs.

teaches: Stand up for the freedom of others to follow their faith
Serve people by digging wells and sharing food
emblems: Wells and community kitchens along his routes
texts: Guru Granth Sahib (116 hymns attributed to him)
Guru Kian Sakhian (a later chronicle that is a source on his life)
festivals: Shaheedi Divas of Guru Tegh Bahadur

facts.text: He carries the titles Hind di Chadar and Srisht di Chadar, meaning shield of India and shield of the world. The Muslim poet Bulleh Shah called him Ghazi, an honorific for a warrior, and Guru Gobind Singh's court poet Sainapati called him protector of humanity.
He was executed on 11 November 1675, yet his Shaheedi Divas is observed in India on 24 November, so the remembrance day and the death date do not match.
Historian Wilfred Smith wrote that the pressure put on the ninth Guru to convert left a deep mark on his nine-year-old son Gobind, who later shaped the Sikhs into the distinct Khalsa community.

When Guru Har Krishan lay ill with smallpox in 1664 and was asked who would lead next, he said only the two words Baba Bakala, meaning the successor was in Bakala. That brief clue let many men there claim the title.
A merchant named Makhan Shah Labana offered two gold coins to each claimant; only Tegh Bahadur remarked that he had promised 500, so Makhan Shah knew he was the Guru.
Makhan Shah then climbed onto a rooftop and shouted that he had found the Guru, in words Sikhs remember as the cry Guru ladho re.
According to the account on the Guru Gobind Singh page, when the Guru weighed going to meet Aurangzeb, his young son Gobind Das told him that no one was more worthy to make that sacrifice.
His son Gobind, later Guru Gobind Singh, was born in Patna in 1666 while the Guru was away in Dhubri, Assam, where a gurdwara now stands, on a journey that also took him to Dhaka.
While he was in Assam, Sikh accounts say he made peace between Raja Ram Singh and the Ahom ruler Raja Chakradhwaj Singha.
His son Guru Gobind Singh wrote in the Bachittar Natak that his father gave up his head but not his honour, and described his death as breaking a pitcher over the emperor's head.

Per Trilochan Singh, 500 Kashmiri Pandits led by Pandit Kirpa Ram came to him at Anandpur. Historian Satish Chandra notes that no writer of the time mentions the persecution they described, so details stay debated.
He composed 116 hymns in 15 ragas, found in the Guru Granth Sahib on pages 219 to 1427; they cover the body, the mind, sorrow, service, death and freedom from attachment.
In the Bachittar Natak, Guru Gobind Singh wrote about his father's sacrifice and added that real men of God do not perform tricks like showmen.
Three companions were executed in front of him in Delhi: they are remembered today as Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dayala.

Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Chandni Chowk stands at the place of his execution; it keeps the preserved trunk of the tree under which he was beheaded and a well he is said to have used for bathing while imprisoned.
Tradition says a disciple burned down his own house at what is now Rakab Ganj Sahib to cremate the Guru's body in secret.
Bhai Jaita, later renamed Bhai Jiwan Singh, carried the Guru's head to Anandpur, where another Sisganj gurdwara marks the cremation.

Sikh tradition says that from prison in Delhi he sent his young son Gobind Das a verse to test whether he was ready to lead; the boy replied with a couplet of his own saying he was ready, and the Guru knew his son was prepared.
As was usual after the execution of Guru Arjan, he was surrounded by armed bodyguards, yet he otherwise lived a plain, simple life.
He left Bakala on pilgrimage in 1656 and was in Patna when Guru Har Rai passed away, so he did not return to Punjab until 1664, about eight years later.
As a boy he trained in archery and horse riding, and was also taught old classics such as the Vedas, the Upanishads and the Puranas.

quiz.q: What does the name Tegh Bahadur roughly mean?
quiz.why: He earned the name after bravery at the Battle of Kartarpur.

quiz.q: Which city did Guru Tegh Bahadur found in the 1660s, first called Chakk Nanaki after his mother?
quiz.why: He bought the land from Rani Champa and founded Anandpur Sahib.

quiz.q: How did Makhan Shah identify the real Guru?
quiz.why: Only Tegh Bahadur noticed that Makhan Shah's offering did not match his promised 500 coins.

quiz.q: What did Makhan Shah shout from the rooftop after finding the Guru?
quiz.why: Sikh tradition says he cried that he had found the Guru, in the words Guru ladho re.
